messages.subject: Multiple iid spatial locations
parts:
Hi,


I’m working on a project trying to relate where fish live to features of the habitat. I have 12 different locations which are all roughly 10 x 20 m areas which are separated by between 250 m and 5 km. I’m trying to build a model using SPDE for this data and have a couple questions about how best to approach it. First, should I build a single mesh that encompasses all the sites, or should I build different meshes for each site and then combine them for the analysis? In the first case how do I properly specify that each site be allowed a different spatial structure within the site (I’ve tried following the example for a space-time model in the SPDE book but I’m uncertain if that is applicable to a space-space model like I have). In the second case (a different mesh for each site) I don’t know how to combine the multiple meshes to be used for the analysis.


I’m also unclear what the difference between groups and blocks is in the context of the inla.spde.make.A function and the n.iid.group in the inla.spde2.pcmatern function and how/if I should be using those.


I’ve attached an R script to simulate something similar to my data and perform the analysis using the method of having a single mesh over the entire area with a finer scale within each site.


Thank you in advance for any advice you have for this!

Jason

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Multiple iid spatial locations
parts:
Hi!

The case "relatively widely separate subregions where we care about
the within-subregion structure" you describe can be approached in
several ways,
but one way that is supported directly is to have a single mesh that
has disconnected components that cover each local region but allows
the same inla analysis code as if it was one connected component with
small triangles at the sites and large triangles connecting them. The
benefit of using disconnected components instead is that one can think
of it as having independent regions that just happen to be modelled
with the same spde parameters using different meshes, and need to
capture only the within-site structure. The between-site variability
can then be approached using other model components (that could be
spde models with only large triangles, or graph/network models, or iid
random effects, etc).

The "group" feature doesn't quite allow this, since it would require
the same mesh for each site; I couldn't work out what the _intent_ of
the code was; I'd need a more mathematical definition of the actual
model you want to implement; there's a lot of syntactically valid code
that implements _some_ model, but it's nicer to have it implement the
model we _want_. ;-)

Instead, to setup such a model you should only need to construct the
disconnected set of boundaries encircling each subregion, which the
inla.noncovex.hull() can do.
Provide points defining the subregions and a "convex" parameter that
gives appropriate domain extension (or if you have a multipolygon
defining the set of boundaries), and approach the mesh building as if
it was one connected domain, with extension of a suitable amount to
avoid boundary effects for each subdomain.

The main downside is that the semi-automated plotting features won't
easily show the local structure, as all subdomains will be plotted, so
you'll need to setup the plotting mapping coordinates more carefully.

It wasn't clear to me if you mentioned the "block" feature because you
think you need it or not? It can be used if your observations are
aggregated over the subregions (but to do that correctly for count
data isn't available yet; it's on our list to construct such
likelihoods in the inlabru package, as they turn into
not-quite-log-linear predictors). But if you're modelling the
structure within the subregions, as I assumed above, then you can
ignore that feature.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Multiple iid spatial locations
parts:
Hi,

Thanks so much for the helpful response!

Easy questions first: “It wasn't clear to me if you mentioned the "block" feature because you think you need it or not?”. I just mentioned the blocks because I was going through the documents and got myself confused thinking about different “mesh blocks” to have different meshes per subregion that are combined. So simply me misinterpreting what the blocks are. You did correctly assume the model I’m aiming for (spatial structure within subregions).

Should I use the inla.nonconvex.hull() function when I already have a multipolygon for the set of boundaries? Visually the meshes created using the multipolygons and inla.nonconvex.hull look more or less the same.

“I'd need a more mathematical definition of the actual model you want to implement; there's a lot of syntactically valid code that implements _some_ model, but it's nicer to have it implement the model we _want_”. Definitely agree with that! First, I’ll try explaining verbally the model I’m aiming for then I’ll try for the math itself.

At each point on a reef within a site I have the number of a species of fish and a handful of covariates relating to the reef structure. Most often there are no fish present, so I want to model the size and presence of the schools of fish using a hurdle model (for the sake of this example I’m using a fixed zero inflation factor but in the final model I’ll model both the presence/absence and the count when present). This model will be based on the measured covariates of the reef along with a random effect of site and a term for the spatial structure which is allowed to vary among sites.

I believe this describes the model I’m trying to fit but I’m definitely still learning how to do all this so please forgive any glaring mistakes!

i = individual data points (1, 2, ..., 2500)

k = sites (1, 2, 3, 4)

j = covariates (0, 1, 2)


y_ik ~ ZIP (lambda_i, pi)

lambda_i = e ^ eta_i

eta_i ~ beta_0 + beta_1 * X_1i + beta_2 * X_2i + mu_ik + gamma_ik

beta_j ~ N(0, 0.001 ^ -1)

gamma_ik ~ GF (0, sigma_k)

sigma_k = Matern covariance

mu_ik ~ N(0, 0.001 ^ -1)

pi ~ U(0, 1)

 

Thank you again for your help!

Jason
